cues.text: Chapter seven turns to one of the newest and most debated areas in technology ethics: generative AI, deepfakes, and a idea called algorithmic colonialism.
Let us begin with generative AI.
Generative AI is a kind of system that produces new text, images, audio or video from patterns it has learned.
It does not simply look something up and hand it back.
It creates new content based on what it has learned from the data it was trained on.
That ability is powerful, but it brings a set of risks that you need to be able to name.
The first risk is fabricated facts.
A system can produce statements that sound confident and fluent but are simply not true.
The second is privacy leakage, where personal information that was in the learning material may surface in what the system produces.
The third is copyright disputes, because questions arise about the material used to teach the system and about the content it generates.
The fourth is discriminatory outputs, where the results treat people or groups unfairly.
And the fifth is misleading synthetic media, meaning artificial text, images, audio or video that can give people a false impression of what is real.
Now consider deepfakes, which are a particularly serious form of synthetic media.
Deepfakes can imitate real people.
That creates four risks you should remember.
The first is fraud, where someone is deceived into handing over money or access.
The second is impersonation, where someone pretends to be another person.
The third is harassment, where the imitation is used to target or demean an individual.
And the fourth is misinformation, where false material about what a person said or did spreads among the public.
But the source is careful to add that this is not the whole picture.
There are legitimate uses.
These can include satire that is clearly labelled, education, accessibility, and creative work, provided there are appropriate rights and safeguards.
So the technology itself is not condemned.
What matters is how it is used, whether people are deceived, and whether rights have been respected.
That leads to the governance question.
A nuanced governance approach distinguishes between two things.
On one side is harmful deception and nonconsensual misuse.
On the other side is legitimate expression.
A blunt rule that treated every synthetic image or voice as wrongful would catch the satirist, the teacher and the accessibility developer along with the fraudster.
A good approach separates them.
What controls might support that approach?
The source lists several.
Consent, where appropriate, for example when a real person's likeness or voice is used.
Clear labelling, so audiences know content is synthetic.
Provenance, which means being able to trace where content came from and how it was made.
Verification channels, so people can check whether something is genuine.
Reporting and removal mechanisms, so that harmful material can be flagged and taken down.
Platform policies, which are the rules that online services set for their own users.
And proportionate enforcement, meaning that the response should fit the seriousness of the wrong.
There is an important warning here.
Watermarks and detection tools are imperfect, so you should not rely on them alone.
A watermark can be missing or removed, and a detection tool can make mistakes, so these tools support a governance approach but cannot be its only foundation.
When you evaluate a particular piece of synthetic content, the source gives you a set of factors to weigh.
Consider the audience, who is going to see it.
Consider the context, where and how it appears.
Consider the likelihood of confusion, whether people could reasonably mistake it for the real thing.
Consider rights, such as those of the person depicted or the owner of the underlying material.
Consider harm, what damage could follow.
And consider legal duties, meaning the obligations that actually apply.
Notice that the last factor is distinct from the others.
An ethical concern is not automatically a legal requirement, so you must check separately what the law requires in the relevant jurisdiction.
Now we move to the second major idea in this chapter: algorithmic colonialism.
This term describes how data extraction, imported models and external control can reproduce unequal power relationships.
The source identifies several ways this can happen.
It can exclude local languages and contexts.
It can concentrate benefits outside the affected communities.
Or it can impose assumptions that are unsuitable for local needs.
It is very important to understand what this concept is and is not.
The source states that it is a critique of power and governance.
It is not a claim that every foreign technology is harmful.
So you should not use the term to reject outside technology automatically.
The concern is about who holds power, who controls decisions, and who benefits.
The source offers two examples.
First, models trained largely outside African contexts may perform poorly on local languages.
Think about what that means in practice.
A tool that works well in one language setting may misunderstand, mistranslate or simply fail for speakers of African languages, leaving them poorly served.
Second, local data may generate value without fair participation or control.
In that situation, data comes from local people and places, but the value it creates flows elsewhere, and the communities involved have little say or share.
So what are the responses?
The source lists several.
Local participation in design and governance, so that affected communities help shape systems rather than merely receive them.
Representative and responsibly collected data, so that the data reflects the people it affects and is gathered properly.
Investment in local expertise, building the skills and institutions that allow communities to develop and oversee technology themselves.
Transparent procurement, so that decisions about acquiring technology are open and accountable.
Appropriate data sovereignty and transfer safeguards, which address who controls data and what protections apply when it moves across borders.
Benefit-sharing, so that value is distributed fairly.
Multilingual accessibility, so that systems work across the languages people actually use.
And accountability, so that someone is answerable when things go wrong.
The source then asks for balance.
International collaboration should be balanced with local autonomy and rights.
Working across borders can bring knowledge and resources, but it should not override the autonomy and rights of local communities.
Finally, there is a caution about one popular answer.
Data localisation alone cannot resolve unequal power or bias.
Data localisation means keeping data within a particular territory.
Keeping data at home may be part of a response, but on its own it does not fix unequal power, and it does not remove bias.
You still need the wider measures we just listed: participation, representative data, local expertise, transparency, benefit-sharing, multilingual access and accountability.
To bring the chapter together, remember the pattern of reasoning.

For generative AI and deepfakes, separate harmful deception and nonconsensual misuse from legitimate expression, apply layered controls, do not depend on watermarks or detection alone, and weigh audience, context, confusion, rights, harm and legal duties.

For algorithmic colonialism, treat it as a critique of power and governance, recognise how exclusion and unfair extraction can occur, and respond through participation, fair benefit and accountability, while balancing international collaboration with local autonomy and rights.
